item.title: Canadian Stage’s A Doll’s House marks the second entry in a trilogy of productions about marriage
item.description: “At 50, thinking about marriage and love, and [their] place in my life, I wanted to do an artistic deep-dive into the idea of partnership,” says director Brendan Healy.

item.title: REVIEW: A Question of Character examines the psychology of a filmmaker who created Nazi propaganda
item.description: The greatest strength of A Question of Character, now playing at the Aki Studio, is that its fundamental questions manifest as an active process. Rather than conveying a pre-packaged conclusion, the production undertakes a genuine attempt to work through Leni Riefenstahl's contradictions while weighing the payoffs of revenge.

item.title: REVIEW: Wet, weird, and woeful, Pu Songling: Strange Tales is a riotous trip into the mystical
item.description: One thing’s for sure — you’ve never seen a show with this much tongue.

item.title: How the Grand Theatre’s Primary Trust makes a tiki bar feel like home
item.description: Let’s get one thing straight: Eboni Booth's Pulitzer-winning Primary Trust isn’t about working in bars. But it honours bars as spaces we return to — where we go to feel safe.

item.title: Q&A: Rick Miller reflects on his one-man multimedia portrait Boom X, now playing at Hamilton’s Theatre Aquarius
item.description: In Boom X, Rick Miller uses theatre to trace how Generation X came of age amid major shifts in media, politics, and daily life from the 1970s through the mid-1990s.

item.title: The new season of PlayME promises five wholehearted Canadian radio dramas about fitting into a weird world
item.description: “Many of the shows this year are about fitting in — being a fish out of water,” says co-creator Chris Tolley. “You can see that explicitly in new immigrant stories, but also in dating stories [about] searching for connection, or even in a piece about a young actor from Toronto trying to assimilate into life on a rural farm.”

item.title: REVIEW: Talk Is Free’s Company is valiant but imperfect
item.description: Playing at The Theatre Centre, it’s an entertaining staging that, like its central character, is still waiting to completely connect.

item.title: REVIEW: In Tarragon and Native Earth’s Mischief, the jokes aren’t the point
item.description: Mischief may not fully cohere into a singular statement, but it leaves behind something quieter and more human: the feeling of having spent time inside a community, listening to its jokes, its arguments, and its silences. It is a play full of questions — some answered, many not — and it trusts the audience enough to live with that uncertainty.

item.title: REVIEW: Canadian Stage’s A Doll’s House weighs the burden of our inherited roles
item.description: Hailey Gillis' Nora is not so much a doll as she is a gifted actor, reeling through daffy comedy, seductive calculation, and suicidal ideation with ease.

item.title: REVIEW: Primary Trust harnesses anxiety for good at London’s Grand Theatre
item.description: Eboni Booth's Pulitzer Prize-winning Primary Trust invites its audience to visualize hopeful futures rather than disasters. This tender production, directed by Cherissa Richards, proposes that imagining such a future is the first step to achieving it.
